title: Jeremiah
subtitle: To uproot and tear down, to build and to plant
lead: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a village a few miles north of Jerusalem. The LORD's word came to him as a young man in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, 627 BC, and he kept speaking it for some forty years: through Josiah's reform and his death in battle (609), the rise of Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, the first deportation to Babylon (597), the long siege and the burning of Jerusalem and its Temple (586), and on into Egypt, where a band of refugees took him against his will. His commission sums up his work: he was set over nations and kingdoms "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant" (1:10).

Jeremiah has more words than any other book of the Bible. It is not arranged by date. Poems of judgment and grief stand beside long prose sermons, stories told about the prophet by someone else, letters, oracles against foreign nations, and a set of prayers in which Jeremiah argues bitterly with God, often called his confessions. Chapter 36 tells how the book began: Jeremiah dictated his words to the scribe Baruch, King Jehoiakim cut the scroll up and burned it column by column, and Jeremiah dictated it again with many words added. The book also survives in two editions, the longer Hebrew text that Jewish and most Christian Bibles translate and a shorter Greek one, and copies of both were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Jeremiah's words outlived the city whose fall he announced. His seventy years of exile (25:11–12; 29:10) shaped the hopes of Daniel and of the Jews who came home under Persia (2 Chronicles 36:21–22; Daniel 9:2). His letter told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they lived (29:7). His promise of a new covenant written on the heart (31:31–34) is quoted in full in Hebrews 8, and Jesus used his phrase "a den of robbers" (7:11) when he drove the traders from the Temple. Jewish tradition makes him the author of Lamentations and of Kings, and his words are read in the synagogue in the weeks before the Ninth of Av, the fast that mourns the Temple.
facts: The book is headed "the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests at Anathoth" (1:1). It says that Jeremiah dictated his messages to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah (36:4, 32), and many of its stories speak of Jeremiah in the third person. The Talmud says that Jeremiah wrote his own book, Kings and Lamentations (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a). Most modern scholars think the book grew from Jeremiah's poetry, prose sermons shaped in the style of Deuteronomy, and stories about him, gathered and edited by his disciples and later scribes (see the authorship section).

Jeremiah was active from 627 BC, Josiah's thirteenth year (1:2), until after the fall of Jerusalem in the summer of 586 BC (some count 587), and his last words were spoken in Egypt (43–44). The book's last event is the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon in 561 BC (52:31). The two editions were probably both complete by the 200s BC.

Jerusalem and Judah in the last forty years of the kingdom: the Temple courts, the palace, the prison yard and the cistern where Jeremiah was held. Then Mizpah under the governor Gedaliah, and Tahpanhes and other towns of Egypt. Assyria was collapsing when the book opens, and Babylon replaced it as master of the region after the battle of Carchemish (605 BC).

Prophecy: oracles in Hebrew poetry (most of 2–20, 30–31 and 46–51), prose sermons (such as 7, 11 and 34), stories about the prophet (26–29, 32–45), symbolic actions, a letter (29), laments and prayers. Chapter 52 is a historical appendix that runs parallel to 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.
Hebrew, with one verse in Aramaic (10:11). The Greek translation was made in Egypt, probably in the 100s BC, from a Hebrew text shorter than the one the Masoretes preserved.
52 chapters, 1,364 verses, about 21,800 Hebrew words: the longest book of the Bible by word count. The Greek edition is about one-seventh shorter.

The Greek lacks about 2,700 words of the Hebrew, and it places the oracles against the nations (Hebrew 46–51) in the middle of the book, after 25:13, in another order. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, two copies (4QJer-b and 4QJer-d) agree with the shorter text and three (4QJer-a, 4QJer-c and 4QJer-e) with the longer. Many scholars, following Emanuel Tov and Pierre-Maurice Bogaert, think the Greek translates an earlier edition of the book, and the Hebrew a later, expanded one; others think the Greek translator or his source shortened it.

4QJer-a from Qumran Cave 4, copied around 200 BC by the usual dating of its handwriting, is one of the oldest of all the scrolls. Six copies in all survive from Qumran (2QJer and 4QJer-a to -e). The Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the base of this translation, is the oldest complete Hebrew copy.

In Jewish Bibles it is the second of the Latter Prophets, after Isaiah, though one Talmud passage puts it first (Bava Batra 14b). In Protestant Bibles it follows Isaiah and comes before Lamentations. Catholic Bibles follow it with Lamentations and Baruch, whose last chapter is the Letter of Jeremiah. Orthodox Bibles, which keep the Greek order, have Jeremiah, Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah.

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads each oracle and scene against the dates the book gives and the events it names: Josiah's reform (622 BC), his death at Megiddo (609), Carchemish (605), the first deportation (597), the siege and fall of Jerusalem (588–586), Gedaliah's murder and the flight to Egypt. It traces how the events Jeremiah announced turned out, including the seventy years.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: the poetry most scholars give to Jeremiah, the prose sermons in the language of Deuteronomy, the stories about him (often credited to Baruch), and the two editions of the book, the longer Hebrew and the shorter Greek with its different order, which Qumran copies show were both in use. It weighs the Babylonian Chronicle, the Lachish and Arad letters and the seals and bullae of the period.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: How the Targum, the rabbis and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Kimchi, Abravanel) read Jeremiah: the prophet of the destruction read on the Ninth of Av, the author by tradition of Lamentations and of Kings (Bava Batra 15a), and the source of the hope of return and of the new covenant.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the New Testament and the church read Jeremiah: the temple sermon in Jesus' cleansing of the temple, Rachel weeping in Matthew 2, the new covenant at the Last Supper and in Hebrews 8, and Jeremiah as a figure of the suffering Christ.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads the promises of return, a righteous Branch from David and a renewed Israel in its land (23:5–8; 30–33) as still waiting for their full fulfillment: in many Christian readings at Christ's return (premillennial and dispensational), and in Jewish hope in the days of the Messiah.

audience.to: Jeremiah first spoke to the people of Judah and Jerusalem between 627 and 586 BC: to crowds at the Temple gates and in its courts, to the kings Jehoiakim and Zedekiah and their officials, to priests and to other prophets, and to the men of his own village. After the city fell he spoke to the survivors at Mizpah and to the Judeans who fled to Egypt, and he wrote to the exiles in Babylon (29). The finished book was read by Jews who had lived through the disaster or grown up after it, in Babylon, in Egypt and in the ruined land of Judah.
audience.why: Before 586 the words were a warning and a summons: Judah had broken its covenant with the LORD, worshiped other gods and wronged the poor, and unless it turned back, a foe from the north would destroy the city and the Temple that the people trusted to protect them. Jeremiah also told kings to submit to Babylon, which made him a traitor in many eyes. After 586 the same words became an explanation and a hope. They told the survivors that the disaster was not the defeat of their God but his judgment, foretold and deserved; that the prophets who had promised peace were liars; and that the LORD who tore down would also build and plant, bring the exiles home after seventy years and make a new covenant with them. Reading the book with both audiences in mind explains why warnings and comfort stand side by side.
views: Jeremiah and Baruch for the generation of the exile

Many scholars, especially conservative ones, think Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch gathered most of the book themselves, beginning with the scroll of 605 BC (36), to warn Judah and then to explain the fall to the exiles; the stories of 26–45 read like the work of an eyewitness close to the prophet (Bright; Thompson; Lundbom, who sees Baruch and his brother Seraiah as the book's first editors).

Many critical scholars think the prose sermons were written or reshaped by later editors in the language of Deuteronomy, to answer the questions of the exiles in Babylon: why had the LORD let Jerusalem fall, and what must they do now? On this view much of the book speaks first to the exile community through Jeremiah's voice (Nicholson; Thiel; Carroll, who thinks little of the book can be traced back to the prophet himself).

Because the shorter Greek edition was translated in Egypt and the longer Hebrew one was completed later, some scholars see the book still being supplemented in the Persian period, perhaps in Babylon or Judah, with additions such as 33:14–26 that answered new questions about David's line and the priests (Tov; Bogaert; Janzen).
